title: How to Stargaze: Sky Maps and Naked-Eye Observing

cards.h: You need no telescope to start
cards.b: From one dark spot, your naked eye can see roughly 2,500 stars, plus planets and the Milky Way as a faint band. Learning to find things is a skill, and it is the first step in astronomy that costs nothing. The sky also teaches rhythm: stars rise about four minutes earlier each night, so the same constellations return at the same time each season.

Your pupils open slowly in the dark. Full dark adaptation takes about 20 to 30 minutes. Phone screens and car lights reset it at once. Use a red torch: the rods in your eye that see faint light are almost blind to red. Light well above 600 nanometres, which looks red to us, barely affects dark-adapted rods.

The centre of your retina is best for colour and detail, but it is poor at faint light. The outer retina has more rods. So a faint star often vanishes when you stare at it and reappears when you look a little to one side. This is averted vision.

cards.h: Find the north with the Big Dipper
cards.b: The two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl, called the pointers, line up with Polaris, the North Star. The distance from the pointers to Polaris is about five times the gap between the pointers. Polaris sits within about one degree of the north celestial pole, so it barely moves.

Stars twinkle because their light is bent by turbulent air. Planets look like tiny discs, so the air evens out their light and they shine steadily. Planets also wander slowly against the background stars over weeks. A sky app, or a paper planisphere set to your date and time, shows you which is which.

A Moon-free night is best for faint objects like the Milky Way. The Milky Way’s bright core is best seen from the northern hemisphere in the warm months, when it rises high in the south. Check the Moon phase and the weather before you go.

Hipparchus, working in the 2nd century BCE, made a star catalogue that is now lost, but his work survives in later copies. Ptolemy’s Almagest, written around 150 CE, lists 1,022 stars. Star maps have always been built by careful naked-eye observation. Galileo's telescope resolved the Milky Way into countless faint stars in 1610, confirming what Ptolemy had seen as a glow.

• 'Stars twinkle because they are small.' Twinkling comes from our atmosphere.
  • 'Polaris is the brightest star.' It is only moderately bright. Sirius is the brightest night star.
  • 'You need a telescope to see anything.' Most of the best sky is visible by eye.
Planets also keep to a narrow band across the sky called the ecliptic, so checking that band helps you spot them.

In Indian tradition the fixed pole star is Dhruva, and the seven sages are the Saptarishi, the stars of the Big Dipper. Indian astronomy also divided the Moon's path into 27 nakshatras, lunar mansions that were used to track time and the Moon's position. You can still find these from a dark terrace.

• Dark adaptation takes 20 to 30 minutes; use red light.
  • Averted vision helps you see faint objects.
  • Pointer stars lead you to Polaris.
  • Planets do not twinkle; stars do.

Think about it: (1) Why does a bright city street hide the Milky Way? (2) Why is Polaris a useful reference only from the northern sky?
